title: Don’t Train From Scratch: Persistent Gains from Pruning-Initialised Distillation for Edge Language Models
content: Mobile robots and autonomous vehicles increasingly use language models for reasoning. On such platforms the embedded accelerator can fix the model's architecture, vocabulary and weight footprint before accuracy is considered. How should such a small model be obtained? We compare three ~360M-parameter student language models. All three learn from one 4.2B-parameter teacher on the same corpus and token budget; they differ in where training starts. Model A, the proposed model, is the teacher's 752M-parameter sibling pruned to the hardware-required size and structure. Model B, a baseline, is an existing public model, SmolLM2-360M, pre-trained on far more data and distilled from teacher-generated text. Model C, the second baseline, has Model A's structure but starts from random weights ("from scratch"). We ask two questions. First, how much do the pruned weights help? Within 1.3B tokens, Model C never reaches the perplexity Model A attains after 100M tokens: a measured token-efficiency advantage above 13x. A saturating fit puts the floor of the perplexity ratio at 1.428. Second, how efficiently does each model turn domain data into domain skill? On a campus-robot scene-understanding task whose answers are checked against ground-truth annotations, every student starts near chance. Under the same adaptation, Model A gains +0.486 in accuracy and Model B +0.142, at a similar cost in general capability. At each model's own best adaptation rate the gains are +0.486 and +0.339, a 1.4x ratio. After pruning and 4-bit weight quantisation the specialist needs 327 MiB of weights, 24x less than the bf16 teacher, with no measurable loss of domain accuracy. In short, we see no sign that any student inherits the teacher's domain skill. Each one must learn from domain data. Given the same data, Model A gains far higher accuracy than Models B and C. Model B, however, keeps the higher scores on general benchmarks.
